title: Body organization, directions and planes
note: Every directional term assumes anatomical position: standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms forward. The terms come in opposite pairs, and right and left always mean the patient's right and left, not the examiner's.

read.title: One body, one reference point
text: Two clinicians describing the same wound need to mean the same thing, so anatomy uses a fixed reference. In anatomical position the body stands upright, faces forward, and has its arms at the sides with the palms turned forward. Every directional term is defined from that stance, even if the patient is actually lying supine on the back or prone on the abdomen.

The terms come in pairs. Anterior and posterior mean front and back. Superior and inferior mean above and below. Medial points toward the midline and lateral points away from it. Proximal and distal are used mainly on limbs: the elbow is proximal to the wrist because it is nearer the trunk. Superficial and deep describe distance from the surface.

Planes are imaginary flat cuts used in imaging and dissection. A sagittal plane separates right from left, a frontal (coronal) plane separates front from back, and a transverse plane separates upper from lower, producing cross-sections.

The abdomen is mapped either into four quadrants or into nine smaller regions. Because right and left always belong to the patient, the appendix sits in the right lower quadrant even though it appears on the examiner's left.
